Corruption: detecting and naming damage

Source: vignettes/corruption.Rmd
corruption.Rmd
library(csvschema)

The wire format assumes a hostile channel: any CSV dialect, any locale, any spreadsheet, any human with find-and-replace. csvschema ships a simulator for every vector in its threat model — the cs_corrupt_*() family — so you can apply a named corruption to a file and watch the reader recover from it, or report exactly what broke.

# A small fixture with values chosen to trip real spreadsheet coercions.
fixture <- data.frame(
  zip    = sprintf("%05d", c(1, 23, 456, 7890, 12345)),  # leading zeros
  bigid  = sprintf("1%015d", 1:5),                        # 16-digit strings
  region = factor(c("NE", "S", "MW", "W", "S")),
  note   = c("SEPT1", "Café", "normal", "0.5", "=SUM(A1)"),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

# Helpers: write the fixture, corrupt the file, read it back.
read_chr <- function(path) {
  read.csv(path, colClasses = "character", check.names = FALSE,
           na.strings = character(0))
}
write_chr <- function(df) {
  tmp <- tempfile(fileext = ".csv")
  utils::write.table(df, tmp, sep = ",", row.names = FALSE, na = "",
                     qmethod = "double", eol = "\n")
  tmp
}

Two layers of protection

The schema packets are protected by a per-packet CRC and a whole-schema hash; the data is protected by the _canary column, which stores a purposeful sample of each variable’s most fragile values plus a fingerprint of the whole column. Recovery and canary results are independent: a file can lose rows (the data changes, the schema survives) or be mangled by a spreadsheet (the schema survives, the data is damaged).

Row loss: schema survives, canary notices

Dropping rows at random leaves the striped, repeated schema intact:

path <- tempfile(fileext = ".csv")
cs_write(fixture, path, verbose = FALSE)

thinned <- cs_corrupt_rows(read_chr(path), keep = 0.5, mode = "random", seed = 1)
out <- cs_read_csv(write_chr(thinned), sidecar = FALSE, verbose = FALSE)
cs_report(out)$status
#> [1] "verified"

Spreadsheet coercion: schema survives, damage is named

cs_corrupt_excel() reproduces what a spreadsheet does on import: it strips leading zeros, renders long digit strings in scientific notation, coerces date-like strings to dates, and turns formula cells into #NAME?. The packets (which begin with {{) match none of those rules, so the schema still verifies — but the canary check finds the damaged values and says which kind of damage hit each variable.

damaged <- cs_corrupt_excel(read_chr(path))
out <- suppressWarnings(cs_read_csv(write_chr(damaged), sidecar = FALSE,
                                    verbose = FALSE))
rep <- cs_report(out)
rep$status                                   # schema still verified
#> [1] "verified"
rep$canary[, c("variable", "verdict", "damage")]
#>   variable   verdict                     damage
#> 1      zip corrupted           leading_zero (4)
#> 2    bigid corrupted            long_digits (5)
#> 3   region    intact                           
#> 4     note corrupted date_like (1); formula (1)

Each damaged variable is mapped back to the detector that selected its lost canary value, so zip reads “leading_zero”, a coerced date reads “date_like”, and so on.

Case folding: detected, not silently wrong

Some mainframe and SQL loaders upper- or lower-case every cell. That folds the packet payloads too, and because each packet’s CRC covers the exact-case payload, the folded packets fail their check and are dropped. The reader does not return a silently wrong schema — it reports the loss:

folded <- cs_corrupt_case(read_chr(path), mode = "upper")
out <- suppressWarnings(cs_read_csv(write_chr(folded), sidecar = FALSE,
                                    verbose = FALSE))
cs_report(out)$status                         # incomplete or absent, never verified
#> [1] "incomplete"

The simulator family

Function What it does
cs_corrupt_rows drop / reorder / duplicate rows
cs_corrupt_columns drop columns; Text-to-Columns split
cs_corrupt_header remove or regenerate the header
cs_corrupt_excel spreadsheet import coercions
cs_corrupt_encoding re-encode (mojibake), NFC/NFD
cs_corrupt_bom prepend a UTF-8 BOM
cs_corrupt_delimiter rewrite the delimiter
cs_corrupt_smartquotes straight quotes to curly, – to em dash
cs_corrupt_whitespace trim, pad, non-breaking spaces
cs_corrupt_truncate truncate every cell
cs_corrupt_case upper / lower / title case
cs_corrupt_merge bind two different schemas
cs_corrupt_eol CRLF / LF swap, drop trailing newline
cs_corrupt_replace global find-and-replace
cs_corrupt_invisible insert zero-width and invisible characters

Each simulator records what it did in a cs_corruption attribute, so a round-trip through several of them is self-documenting:

x <- cs_corrupt_rows(read_chr(path), keep = 0.5, seed = 1)
attr(cs_corrupt_excel(x), "cs_corruption")
#> [1] "rows(mode=random, keep=0.5)" "excel()"
